concept: Substituting a generic, wordplay-driven, or unrelated management idea for the source's one specific, named 'cardinal rule' of cost control (that control-technique cost must be less than the money it saves).

concept: Conflating two independent judgments that must be made separately: (1) cost status (overrun/underrun), which compares actual cost to EARNED value, and (2) unit-rate performance (better/worse), which compares the actual unit rate to the budget unit rate, where a LOWER actual rate is favorable.
description: Distractors either compare actual cost to the wrong benchmark (full total budget instead of earned value, producing a false 'under run' read), or invert the unit-rate performance direction (treating a lower, more efficient actual rate as 'worse'), or both -- the two determinations must each be made against their own correct benchmark.

concept: Applying the source's no-actual-cost-data placeholder default (CPI = 1.00) to a situation where real, unequal BCWP/ACWP figures are actually given, or assuming multiple accounts' variances simply net to that default without summing the underlying figures.
description: CPI = 1.00 is defined as a placeholder used only in the absence of actual cost data; once real BCWP and ACWP figures exist (individually or in aggregate across several accounts), the index must be computed from them and the no-data default no longer applies.

concept: Reporting only one of the two required additive terms in an EAC formula that sums actual cost to-date and a remaining-work term (e.g., unit-rates Method 1: EAC = Actual Cost + (To-go Qty x Budget Unit Rate)), omitting the other term entirely.

concept: Treating one EAC forecasting method as universally superior, cherry-picking whichever method yields the most favorable number, or deferring EAC forecasting altogether -- contrary to the source's guidance to run all methods together and report the full range early.

concept: Substituting a plausible-sounding but undefined term for one of the source's three specifically named EAC forecasting methods (Method 1: budget rate; Method 2: performance-to-date continues/cumulative rate to-date; Method 3: historical curves).
description: Each of the three methods has a specific defined basis; distractors substitute an unstated concept (e.g., 'supervisor prediction') for one method's name, or substitute one method's basis (e.g., 'last period rate') for a different method's actual defined basis (budget rate or cumulative-to-date rate), producing a plausible but incorrectly-labeled trio.

concept: Restating the original, unadjusted budget (BAC) unchanged as the EAC, ignoring both the actual cost already incurred and the required remaining-work or CPI-based adjustment that the applicable EAC formula (Method 1 or Method 2) specifies.
description: Once real actual-cost data exists, an EAC formula always incorporates that actual cost and/or a performance-based adjustment (CPI); an EAC value that exactly equals the original budget, unmodified, cannot be a valid application of any defined EAC method once actual performance data is available.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting an incomplete sentence fragment or a plausible-sounding paraphrase for the source's specific stated advantage of the earned value method (comparability to the value of work scheduled, within an integrated project control system).
description: The source names one specific comparability advantage for the earned value method; distractors substitute a different, textually inaccurate comparison point (e.g., unit cost, or a paraphrase like 'schedule percent complete') that does not match the source's actual wording.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Reporting a status measure of work performed to date (earned value/BCWP) as if it were itself a forward-looking forecast of total cost at completion (EAC).
description: Earned value measures accomplishment to date and answers a fundamentally different question than EAC, a forward-looking projection of total cost; a distractor that simply restates the earned-value figure from the same scenario as the 'EAC' confuses a status measure with a forecast.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Summing raw physical quantities completed across multiple rules-of-credit subtasks (or using only one subtask's raw quantity) without applying each subtask's defined weight, when computing total equivalent units for a multi-step activity.
description: Equivalent units under the rules-of-credit method require summing (weight x units done) across ALL listed subtasks; distractors either add the raw quantities of all subtasks with no weighting at all, or use only a single subtask's raw quantity while ignoring the others and all weights.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Treating a cost-efficiency index (CPI = EV/AC) as if it directly measured what fraction of total scope has been completed, when percent complete is actually a separate, unrelated ratio (EV/BAC).
description: CPI and percent-complete are built from different pairs of quantities and answer different questions (cost efficiency vs. scope completion); a CPI value of e.g. 0.85 carries no information about what percentage of the account's scope is finished.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Consistently reversing the operand order in all four EVM formulas at once (SV, SPI, CV, CPI), producing a fully self-consistent but entirely wrong set of values because earned value is never placed first/on top as each formula requires.
description: This is the compound, all-four-formulas form of the sign/reciprocal-reversal error: SV uses PV-EV instead of EV-PV, SPI uses PV/EV instead of EV/PV, CV uses AC-EV instead of EV-AC, and CPI uses AC/EV instead of EV/AC, so every value is either sign-flipped or the reciprocal of the correct one, though internally consistent with itself.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Attributing the source's stated advantage of one of the two named labor cost control reporting systems (earned value method / unit rates method) to the other system.
description: The source names each system's advantage separately and specifically (earned value's advantage is integration/comparability with scheduled value; unit rates' advantage is familiarity from estimating use); a distractor swaps one system's stated advantage onto the other.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Computing an EVM/productivity ratio (CPI, SPI, UCI, or PI) with numerator and denominator reversed, producing the mathematical reciprocal of the correctly defined index -- and often mislabeling the resulting value's favorable/unfavorable or ahead/behind direction to match.
description: Every ratio index in this chapter (CPI=EV/AC, SPI=EV/PV, UCI=Credit$/Actual$, PI=CreditWH/ActualWH) is defined with the 'earned'/'credit' quantity always as the numerator; distractors that invert the ratio produce its exact reciprocal, sometimes correctly reproduced across one, several, or all four indices in a single multi-part item, and the interpretive label may or may not be adjusted to match the inverted number.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.
notes: skill_id set to the most common associated skill (EARNED_VALUE_ANALYSIS, 4/8 rows); this misconception recurs across multiple skill/topic areas (['EARNED_VALUE_ANALYSIS', 'PRODUCTIVITY_MEASUREMENT', 'UNIT_COST_ANALYSIS']) -- individual diagnostic rows carry their own item-specific skill_id, which is what fragility/retest logic actually uses.

concept: Either multiplying crew size into an already-crew-total labor-hour figure a second time (double-counting), or omitting the crew-size factor entirely from a total labor-cost calculation (computing as if only one worker were being paid).
description: Total labor-hours needed (Quantity/Productivity) already represents the whole crew's combined effort; correctly finding total labor cost requires exactly one multiplication by wage rate and no re-multiplication by crew size, while a duration-based cost calculation (Days x Hours/day x Wage) requires crew size as a fourth, separate factor that must not be dropped.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting items from the source's separate list of factors AFFECTING PRODUCTIVITY (crew size, craft density, scheduling, materials, rework, weather, etc.) for the three specifically defined COMPONENTS OF LABOR COST (quantities installed, production rates, wage rates).
description: The source maintains two distinct enumerated lists for two different questions; a distractor answering 'what are the components of labor cost' with items drawn from the productivity-factors list conflates a determinant of performance with the cost formula's own structural components.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting an unrelated calculation (e.g., averaging total project cost across accounts, or a different Ch.19 formula such as Credit Dollars) -- or denying the derivation is possible at all -- for the source's specific, directly-stated method of converting workhours to labor dollars (Dollars = Workhours x Wage Rate).
description: The source states plainly that labor dollars are derived by multiplying each workhour by its applicable wage rate; distractors substitute a genuinely different Ch.19 formula that produces dollars from a different input (Credit Dollars = Actual Qty x Budget Unit Cost), an unrelated averaging calculation, or an outright denial that any such derivation exists.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a pair of scheduling/network techniques, or a real Ch.19 sub-metric, for the source's two specifically named labor cost control reporting systems (the earned value method and the unit rates method).
description: The source names exactly two prevalent labor cost control reporting systems; distractors substitute unrelated scheduling-diagramming technique pairs (bar chart/CPM, ADM/PDM) or a real but different-scope Ch.19 metric (the Productivity Index, itself a sub-calculation WITHIN the earned value system, not a reporting system in its own right).
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Redefining the learning-curve percentage as something other than a rate of improvement in labor time per unit triggered by cumulative output doubling -- e.g., as a cap on production capacity, or as a fixed-calendar-interval cost reduction.
description: The learning-curve percentage is specifically triggered by cumulative OUTPUT doubling and describes DECLINING labor time per unit; distractors substitute an unrelated operational constraint (capacity limiting) or an incorrect trigger mechanism (elapsed calendar time rather than cumulative production).
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Describing the learning curve as a flat, unit-to-immediately-previous-unit ratio (the UNIT learning-curve model) when the source specifically defines the CUMULATIVE-AVERAGE model, where the percentage applies to the cumulative average time whenever cumulative quantity doubles.
description: Two distinct, real learning-curve conventions exist in the broader field (unit model vs. cumulative-average model); the source specifically defines the cumulative-average convention, so a technically-real description of the OTHER convention is still incorrect as an answer about THIS source's defined model.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Broadening the source's specific management-by-exception focus (concentrating corrective effort on activities/accounts that DEVIATE from budget) into uniform attention across an entire organizational level (every WBS level, the whole project, or the account level in general).
description: The source specifies that the project manager targets deviating activities specifically, not a uniform scope of review; distractors substitute a broader, non-targeted scope (every WBS level, the aggregate project total, or the account level generally including on-budget accounts) that would dilute or hide the deviations the source says to target.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Using an inconsistent, contradicted-by-the-facts, or one-sided basis when computing project margin -- e.g., citing a driver the scenario explicitly rules out, using a stale original budget after cost is known to have changed, or applying only one side (cost or revenue) of a single approved change.
description: Correct margin analysis requires an internally consistent basis: the driver named must match the facts actually stated in the scenario, the cost figure used must be the current forecast once known to have changed, and a single change's cost and revenue impacts must be applied together, not asymmetrically.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Treating a cost or revenue driver the scenario explicitly names (an approved change, a material escalation, a productivity variance) as having no effect on margin, reporting only one side of its financial impact, excluding it from the analysis altogether, or reporting it in isolation without connecting it to margin.
description: Margin analysis must identify, quantify, and net together ALL known cost/revenue drivers the scenario states; a known driver cannot be assumed to have zero effect, have only its favorable side counted, be excluded because it is 'separately authorized,' or be reported as a standalone figure disconnected from its margin consequence.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Transposing two distinct, correctly-computed quantities into each other's positions within a multi-field EVM worksheet answer (e.g., swapping BCWP and CWH), while leaving other fields (like a ratio computed from the pre-swap values) internally inconsistent with the swap.
description: In a multi-value worksheet answer, each field has its own distinct formula and correct value; a transposition distractor presents two genuinely correct individual values but in each other's slots, which can be detected because a downstream ratio field (e.g., CPI) still reflects the correct, pre-swap pairing rather than being recomputed from the swapped values.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a different, unrelated named management or economics concept (Peter Principle, law of diminishing returns) or an unrelated Ch.19 term (rules of credit) for Pareto's Law/the 80-20 principle the source specifically names for cost control.
description: The source specifically invokes Pareto's Law (80% of outcome from 20% of elements) as the basis for approaching cost control; distractors substitute a different named concept that sounds similarly authoritative but describes an unrelated phenomenon (career-hierarchy incompetence, declining marginal returns, or progress-crediting mechanics).
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a subjective estimate, or a formula built from the wrong pair of quantities (hours instead of quantity, or budgeted instead of forecasted total), for the source's specific defined percent-complete formula (actual quantity divided by forecasted total quantity).
description: Percent complete under the earned value method is a defined, objective ratio of actual QUANTITY to forecasted total QUANTITY; distractors substitute a subjective management estimate, or swap in hours for quantity and/or 'budgeted' for 'forecasted,' each changing the formula's actual defined inputs.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Misplacing the decimal point when converting a given percentage to a fraction before multiplying it by a budget or total figure (e.g., treating 25% as division by 100 or 25% as 0.03), producing a result an order of magnitude too small.
description: Formulas like BCWP = %Complete x Budget and BCWS = Scheduled %Complete x Budget require converting the given percentage to its correct decimal fraction (25% to 0.25, 30% to 0.30) before multiplying; distractors apply an incorrect conversion (dividing by 100 without the fraction step, or shifting the decimal one place too far) that yields a value roughly 1/10th the correct one.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.
notes: skill_id set to the most common associated skill (EARNED_VALUE_ANALYSIS, 2/5 rows); this misconception recurs across multiple skill/topic areas (['EARNED_VALUE_ANALYSIS', 'NET_PROFIT_MARGIN_CALCULATION', 'ROA_DIRECT_CALCULATION', 'ROI_CALCULATION']) -- individual diagnostic rows carry their own item-specific skill_id, which is what fragility/retest logic actually uses.

concept: Reducing the source's multi-item list of named factors affecting craft productivity to a single, source-unlisted item (wage rate, accounting software, contract type alone) framed as the ONLY recognized factor.
description: The source names a specific set of field/site-condition factors affecting productivity (crew size, density, interference, scheduling, materials, rework, layout, weather, constructability); distractors substitute a single unlisted item -- often one belonging to a genuinely different Ch.19 topic (labor cost, cost-coding software, contractual risk allocation) -- framed as the sole recognized factor, which both narrows and misattributes the list.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Computing a raw actual-output-per-actual-input rate (ignoring the budget benchmark entirely) and presenting it as if it were the Productivity Index, which specifically compares budget-rate-credited output to actual input.
description: PI = CreditWH/ActualWH, where CreditWH is actual quantity valued at the BUDGET production rate -- a comparison against a benchmark; a raw actual-output/actual-input rate (ActualQty/ActualWH) ignores the budget rate entirely and is a fundamentally different, benchmark-free quantity, not merely a computational variant of PI.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a plausible-sounding but source-unstated physical or organizational attribute (height, supervisor willingness, intangibility) for the source's one specific stated factor making construction quantity measurement more or less difficult (whether an item is installed in one step or several).
description: The source names one specific factor governing measurement difficulty (single-step vs. multi-step installation); distractors substitute an unrelated attribute that sounds plausible as a measurement-difficulty factor but is never the one the source actually identifies.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Attributing a cost overrun to a unit-rate cause (a change in wage rate, equipment rental rate, or overtime premium -- each of which changes cost PER UNIT) while mislabeling it as a quantity variance cause (more units installed than budgeted).
description: The source attributes cost overruns to two distinct causes -- quantities installed exceeding budget (a quantity variance, from scope/takeoff/rework issues) versus the actual per-unit rate exceeding budget (a rate variance, from wage/equipment/overtime rate changes); a distractor correctly identifies a real cause of overrun but misclassifies a rate-driven cause as a quantity-driven one.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Reporting a different step's individual percentage, a cumulative running total across multiple completed steps, or full-activity (100%) credit, instead of the single step's own specifically defined percentage credit under a rules-of-credit scheme.
description: Each subtask/step in a rules-of-credit scheme earns its own specifically defined percentage; distractors substitute a different step's percentage, sum several steps' percentages into a cumulative total when only one step's marginal credit is asked for, or claim full completion (100%) when only one of several required steps is actually done.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a plausible-sounding but source-unstated rationale, or a stated consequence mistaken for the actual stated cause, for the source's one specific given reason behind a claim (e.g., why labor cost control matters).
description: The source gives one specific stated reason for a claim (labor costs are the most VARIABLE budget element, making their control paramount to profitability); distractors substitute a different, plausible-sounding characteristic never actually claimed by the source (visibility, involving people) or mistake a stated CONSEQUENCE of the reason (profitability) for the reason itself.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Substituting a general communication practice, a generic software tool, or an absurd unrelated instrument for the source's one specific named analytical method (two-way variance analysis) used to allocate a budget-vs-EAC difference to a quantity or rate cause.
description: The source names a specific analytical method for answering who/what is responsible for a total budget-to-EAC difference; distractors substitute a general practice (update meetings), a generic tool (cost-tracking software) that could perform calculations but is not itself the named analytical method, or a wholly unrelated and implausible instrument.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Reporting the raw budget/forecast base totals, or a total net variance used only as a decomposition check figure, as if either were the Quantity Variance or Rate Variance themselves, instead of computing the two-way decomposition's own defined difference formulas.
description: Quantity Variance = (QB-QF)xPB and Rate Variance = QFx(PB-PF) are each specific difference formulas, not the raw QxP base totals (QBxPB, QFxPF) the decomposition starts from, nor the single net total-variance check figure (Budget total - Forecast total) their sum should equal; distractors substitute one of these related-but-distinct figures for the actual variance components.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Reversing the subtraction order within one or both of the two-way variance formulas (Quantity Variance, Rate Variance), producing values with the correct magnitude but the opposite (favorable/unfavorable) sign.
description: Quantity Variance = (QB-QF)xPB and Rate Variance = QFx(PB-PF) each require the BUDGET quantity/rate to come first in their subtraction; reversing this order in one or both formulas produces the correctly-magnituded but sign-flipped variance, misreporting a favorable result as unfavorable or vice versa.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Using the account's raw total Budget directly in place of the required intermediate Credit Dollars figure (Actual Qty x Budget Unit Cost) when computing the Unit Cost Index, sometimes compounded with also inverting the resulting ratio.
description: UCI requires first computing Credit$ = Actual Qty x Budget Unit Cost, THEN dividing by Actual$; skipping this quantity-scaling step and using the raw account Budget total instead of Credit$ is only coincidentally correct when forecast quantity equals budget quantity, and is wrong in general -- this error can also compound with a numerator/denominator inversion.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Attributing schedule-position information (ahead of/behind schedule) to the Unit Cost Index, which measures unit-rate cost efficiency in isolation from quantity and carries no schedule information at all.
description: UCI (Credit$/Actual$) is a unit-rate cost-efficiency measure with no relationship to schedule position; only SPI (EV/PV), which requires separate PV/BCWS data, speaks to whether an account is ahead of or behind schedule -- attaching a schedule-status interpretation to a correctly-computed UCI value confuses two unrelated index domains.
retest_requirement: A different canonical item, independent evidence family, answered correctly at medium/high confidence resolves this misconception; the same item or same evidence family answered correctly does not.

concept: Attributing the source's empirical median finding on cost-account count (from a specific study) to a fictitious government regulation, an absolute measurement necessity, or a generic accounting-principle requirement, and/or misidentifying the underlying reason many accounts are needed as anything other than the lack of a common unit of measure for construction outputs.
description: The source presents the ~400-account figure as an empirical median from a specific study of a specific project size, and explains the underlying need for many cost accounts as arising because outputs (unlike dollar/workhour inputs) lack a common unit of measure; distractors invent a regulatory, absolute-necessity, or generic-accounting-standard justification, or substitute an unrelated purpose (creating work, poor planning, error reduction) for the source's actual stated reason.
